note: Peer reviewed architecture taxonomy covering training pipelines, datasets and deployment issues in one place.
title: A Review on Large Language Models: Architectures, Applications, Taxonomies, Open Issues and Challenges
authors: Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan et al.

reading.body:
This 2024 review consolidates LLM architectures, training pipelines, datasets, and deployment problems into a single taxonomy, drawing on 801 prior works to map the complete landscape of how these systems are built and where they fail in practice.

The paper structures what is otherwise scattered across thousands of publications. It traces LLM development from foundational concepts through transformer architecture to actual training methodologies and the datasets used. It then documents real applications in healthcare, education, and other fields alongside the concrete technical and practical obstacles that prevent reliable deployment. This organization matters because it exposes what researchers still need to solve before LLMs can operate reliably at scale across different domains.

For compute and infrastructure strategy, the value lies in what the paper does not claim to answer. A taxonomy of architectures and training pipelines reveals the computational steps required, but a survey of existing literature cannot itself quantify the power or cooling demands these systems impose, nor can it predict how those demands will change as model sizes or training methods evolve. The paper documents what is broken in deployment, but addresses open issues rather than solutions, so it identifies constraints without predicting when they will be solved.

This work serves as a reference map rather than a roadmap. It shows where the field stands and what remains unsolved, which is useful for organizations deciding whether to adopt LLMs now or wait for maturation. It does not project timelines or resource requirements for the maturation itself.

explain_beginner: This paper does not run a new experiment, instead it asks a mapping question, given how fast large language models have multiplied since ChatGPT's release, can one document pull together how they are built, trained, used, and where they still fall short, in a way a newcomer or a busy practitioner can actually use? Raiaan and coauthors trace the history of these text generating AI systems from earlier language models up through the transformer based systems in wide use today, explain the standard pipeline of pretraining then fine tuning then alignment with human feedback, and catalog real applications across fields including healthcare, education, agriculture, and business. The review found that despite the pace of progress, unresolved problems, like factual errors the model states confidently, high computational cost, and difficulty adapting safely to sensitive domains, show up repeatedly across nearly every application area they surveyed. As a review rather than new research, it does not itself resolve any of these open problems, it organizes and names them so future work has a clearer target.
explain_business: For a team trying to get oriented before making an AI investment decision, this kind of review is useful as a single reference point that lays out what current large language models can plausibly do well, translation, summarization, question answering, code assistance, against the practical constraints, inference cost, hallucination risk, and domain adaptation difficulty, that determine whether a specific use case is ready to deploy now or needs more groundwork first. It is explicitly not a source of new performance numbers or a comparison of specific vendor models, so it should not be used to pick between competing products. Its business value is in scoping conversations, helping a team new to this technology understand which problems, like factual reliability or high serving cost, are known, active, unsolved research areas rather than something a vendor's product update will quietly fix, and which application domains, per the survey's own examples in healthcare and education, already have documented deployment patterns worth learning from before committing budget.
explain_practitioner: This is a structured survey rather than an empirical study, it synthesizes the large language model literature along five threads, historical evolution from earlier neural language models to current transformer architectures, the mechanics of the transformer itself, the standard three stage training pipeline of pretraining, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback, the datasets and compute resources that pipeline depends on, and deployment patterns across domains including biomedical and healthcare, education, agriculture, and general business use. Because it is a review, there is no single benchmark result or baseline comparison to report, its contribution is the taxonomy itself and the systematic cataloging of open issues, which the authors group by technical causes, hallucination, high inference and training cost, limited context handling, and by practical deployment barriers, data privacy, domain adaptation, and evaluation gaps. The authors' own framing acknowledges the review's core limitation, a field moving this fast means any single snapshot taxonomy risks being outdated by the time newer architectures or training techniques become standard practice.
